You are a professional biblical lexicographer fluent in Spanish. Translate the following English lexicon entry into Spanish.

Lemma: H6210

ENGLISH GLOSSES TO TRANSLATE:
  Terse gloss: "A couch or bed for sleeping, reclining, or rest; ranges from an ordinary sleeping bed to a luxurious divan or sickbed"
  Readable gloss: "Refers to a piece of furniture for lying down, whether for nightly rest, lavish banqueting, or convalescence. In Amos 3:12 and 6:4 the prophet pairs it with mittah to condemn the idle rich sprawled on ornate divans, a picture the Spanish 'lechos' and French 'lit' both capture with their connotation of luxury bedding. In Deuteronomy 3:11 Og's famous iron eres may denote a massive bedstead or even a funerary sarcophagus. The Psalms use the same word for the tear-soaked bed of grief (Ps 6:6) and the sickbed where the Lord sustains the afflicted (Ps 41:3)."

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "bed or couch for sleeping"
    Enriched: The ordinary bed or couch used for sleeping at night. Most languages render this straightforwardly — English 'my bed,' Spanish 'mi lecho,' French 'mon lit.' Job 7:13 and Psalm 6:6 both show a sufferer seeking comfort or weeping on this nightly resting place, while Proverbs 7:16 and Song of Solomon 1:16 lend it an intimate, domestic quality.
    Existing Spanish translations: lecho-mío, mi-lecho, mi-lecho,, nuestro-lecho, su-cama
  Sense 2: "bedstead or bier"
    Enriched: A large bedstead or bed-frame, possibly doubling as a funerary bier. The landmark example is Og's iron eres in Deuteronomy 3:11, whose enormous dimensions suggest a royal or commemorative piece of furniture. Psalm 132:3 pairs it with yetsuai ('my spread-out bed'), intensifying the image of a formal resting-place. BDB notes the possible transfer to a sarcophagus — the 'last couch.'
    Existing Spanish translations: cama-de
  Sense 3: "luxurious couch or divan"
    Enriched: A luxurious couch or divan for reclining in ease. Amos 3:12 and 6:4 place this word alongside mittot ('beds') to depict Israel's wealthy lounging in self-indulgent comfort. Spanish consistently renders both occurrences with 'lecho/lechos,' while English uses 'couch/couches,' both preserving the note of opulence that fuels the prophetic rebuke.
    Existing Spanish translations: lecho, sus-lechos
  Sense 4: "sickbed"
    Enriched: A sickbed — the bed upon which one lies during illness. In Psalm 41:3 the Lord 'sustains him on his sickbed' (eres devai). English 'bed of,' Spanish 'lecho de,' and French 'lit' all point to the same concrete image, but the context of suffering and divine care distinguishes this sense from ordinary sleeping.
    Existing Spanish translations: lecho-de
